units: the writer addresses an acquaintance who had left a device with him
he takes the old device out of a cupboard and looks it over
he has just bought a recent model of the same kind
the old device weighs twice as much as the recent one
its metal shell warms up while it is being used
the screen of the recent model renders colours better
the old device opens up so that its battery can be replaced
the recent model is glued together and does not open
the writer asks his correspondent for a reply
text: Do you still think about that tablet you left with me before you went away? I dug it out of the cupboard last night and stood it beside the one I have only just bought, and the gap between the two made me laugh out loud. The old one weighs twice as much, and its thick metal shell warms up under your fingers the moment you open a second window. The recent one slips into a coat pocket, and its screen shows colours the older machine never managed. Still, I will say one thing for the old tablet: it can be mended. I have unscrewed the back myself to fit a fresh battery, whereas the later model is glued shut and will not come apart without cracking. One wins on lightness, the other on good behaviour. Guess which one stays on my desk. Write back and tell me what you make of it before you come home.

units: excess heat is what wears portable computers most
the dust that gathers blocks the air vents
that blockage stops the fan from cooling the machine
the device slows itself down to protect itself
a steady or crackling sound announces the fault
the keyboard turns hot to the touch
the computer slows down for no visible reason
the power must be cut before the casing is opened
replacing the fan costs little and is done in a single job
text: What wears out a portable computer fastest? Heat, says the repair workshop that takes us in. And where does the heat come from? From dust, which mats the vents, stops the fan turning and forces the machine to throttle itself. What warns you before the failure? Three signs, and they recur. Sound first: a steady rush of air, then a crackle as the blades catch their housing. Then the keyboard, which turns warm under your hands. Last, the slowness, which settles in with no visible cause. What should you do? Cut the power, unscrew the base plate, blow the dust outwards and screw it back. And if the noise stays? The fan needs replacing, a cheap job the workshop finishes in a single visit. Should you open it yourself? The engineer hesitates, then says a careful hand beats a smothered machine.

units: a repairer announces that she has found the fault
the person in charge of the place questions her about her diagnosis
a blinking coloured light put her on the trail
she cleaned away a corroded deposit on the board
she soldered back a conductor that had come loose
she warns that the machine must be kept away from the wall
otherwise the hot air gathers behind the device
the person in charge undertakes to move it the next day
the device lights up again once reassembled and plugged in
text: The engineer set her bag on the bench and said she had found the fault. The manager asked her what she had seen. She told him that an amber light had been blinking as soon as she lifted the casing, and that this had put her on the trail. Then she explained how she had taken out the board, scraped away a greenish crust along one track, and soldered back a wire that had been hanging loose. The manager wanted a promise. She answered that the joint would hold if the workshop stopped pressing the machine against the wall, since the hot air had nowhere to go behind it. He said he would shift it the following morning. She closed the lid, put the four screws back in the order she had laid them out, and plugged the machine back in while he stood there watching. The screen came on, a pale blue.

units: the old calculating machines worked with toothed wheels
every added wheel raised the mechanical resistance
that resistance bent the shafts that carried the movement
the number of columns therefore stayed limited
the makers wanted to do away with the moving parts
the electromechanical switch avoided gearing but wore out
it also made a sharp noise at every calculation
the vacuum tube was fast but gave off a great deal of heat
that thermal constraint led on to the solid component
text: Before electricity, adding by machine meant toothed wheels linked by pawls. Every wheel added friction, the friction called for a firmer push on the crank, and that push ended by bending the shafts. Hence the limit of such machines: past a dozen columns, the gearing jammed. Makers therefore set out to get rid of the moving part. The electromechanical relay gave them a first way out, since it switched without gears; but its contacts wore away, and its clack gave away every sum. The vacuum tube came next: quicker, and silent, yet it ran so hot that each cabinet needed its own fan and a steady supply of replacements for the burnt-out bulbs. It was that heat, as much as the cost, that pushed the workshops towards the solid component, cold, tiny, and free of anything that moves.

units: a battery that runs down early is not necessarily worn out
three habits account for the quick draining
a display kept at full brightness draws the most
some programs reach the network without being used
heat lowers the capacity of the cell for good
it is advised to lower the brightness and let it be set automatically
the updating of unused programs must be switched off
leaving the device on charge all night harms the battery
these moves put off the battery change without restoring it
text: A battery that runs flat before evening worries its owner, though wear seldom explains it. Three habits account for most cases. The first is a screen kept at full brightness, since the panel draws more than the processor does. The second is the long list of programs that reach for the network in the background, unopened. The third is heat, because a warm cell loses capacity for good. The answer falls into three moves. Lower the brightness first, and let the device set it by itself. Then switch off background refreshing for the programs you hardly ever open. Finally, keep the machine out of direct sun, and stop leaving it on the charger all night, since a cell held at the top of its range grows tired. None of this hands back a fresh cell, but it does put off the day of replacement.

units: two staff from one department are each given a pilotless flying machine
these craft are used to inspect the roofs of buildings
one of the models is heavy and can be mended on the spot
the other model is compact and easy to carry
any breakage of the compact model means sending it back to the maker
a gust comes up during the first outing
the compact craft drifts off and strikes a water channel
one of its blades snaps
its user waits two weeks for the spare part
the two machines are now used according to how exposed the site is
text: Two colleagues on the same maintenance team were handed a flying machine each in the same week, both meant for inspecting roofs. One picked a sturdy model with a thick moulded frame, whose blades can be swapped by hand in a moment. The other preferred a light craft that folds into a pocket, quicker to get airborne, though the smallest broken part means sending the whole thing back to the maker. During the first inspection the wind got up. The heavy machine held its place above the timbers while the light one drifted and struck a gutter. A blade snapped clean off. Its owner waited a fortnight for a part his colleague kept in the boot of his van. Since then, the heavy model goes up on exposed sites and the light one in sheltered yards, and they no longer argue about which is better.

units: the power must be cut before anything is handled
this precaution is presented as one that cannot be undone
a working surface has to be laid out beforehand
the tools include a fine screwdriver and a pair of flat pliers
a small container serves to keep the screws
the corner screws come out before those along the edges
the screws differ in length and their positions must be noted
a flexible ribbon joins the cover to the electronic board
a charging light that stays dark accuses the socket more often than the battery
text: Kill the power and pull the charger out before you touch anything: that is the one step you cannot undo. Then get your corner of the table ready. You want a fine screwdriver, a pair of flat pliers, a dry cloth and a small dish for the screws, or they roll off and you end up on your knees. Start at the back of the machine. Take the corner screws out first, then the ones along the edges, and note where each came from, because they are not all the same length. Lift the cover gently, never with a jerk, since a soft ribbon usually joins it to the board. Now look at the charging light: if it stays dark, the fault sits in the socket far more often than in the battery. Clean, put it back together, do the screws up without forcing, plug in, and watch the screen before you tidy up.

units: a fault in the sound at a station is reported before sunrise
the departure board then went out altogether
maintenance staff reach the plant room shortly afterwards
a backup power unit had shut itself down for protection
its red lamp stayed lit without blinking
a stalled fan had let the cabinet heat past the limit
the staff changed the fan and cleaned the filters
the board was brought back platform by platform
management now requires the cabinets to be checked every quarter
some travellers missed a change of train for want of information
text: The call came in shortly before dawn: a crackle in the loudspeakers of a station, and then the departure board going dark from end to end. A maintenance team reached the plant room half an hour later. They found first that a backup supply had shut itself down, its red lamp steady rather than blinking. By midday the cause was plain: a stalled fan had let the cabinet climb past the temperature at which everything cuts out. The team fitted a replacement fan, cleared the filters and brought the power back in the early afternoon. The board returned platform by platform, in the reverse order of its going out. Management announced that same evening that the cabinets would be inspected every quarter instead of once a year. No train ran late, but travellers missed connections for want of an announcement.

units: an adjustable light is aimed at the working surface
printed boards are stacked up waiting to be mended
a pencil mark shows the burnt patch on each board
the soldering tool rests in its cradle and still gives off smoke
the smell of resin has soaked into the walls of the room
the craftsman has done this work since the shop opened
runs of melted metal have marked the floor
the seat has left four pale round marks
the lack of a window calls for constant air extraction
the noise stopping signals a break in the power supply
text: On the mender's bench, a jointed lamp leans down over an orderly sort of mess. Green boards are waiting in a stack, each one carrying a pencil stroke where the circuit has darkened and blistered. To the right, the iron rests in its cradle, and its thin tip is still smoking with the smell of warm resin. That smell has soaked deep into the walls, for the man has been soldering here since the day the shop first opened. The floor carries the trade as well: drops of solder have melted into the covering, and the stool has worn four pale rings. Since the room has no window at all, an extractor turns above the door without pause, and its drone ends up passing for silence. When it stops, the man lifts his head, because that hole in the sound means the power has gone and the joint will be spoilt.

units: putting something right often costs more than buying it new
the writer blames this imbalance on the way products are designed
a battery held on with adhesive makes the taking apart harder
screws with an unusual head call for tools kept for them alone
a soldered link instead of a plug lengthens the job
the makers justify these choices by water resistance
a compressed seal and ordinary screws would hold just as well
the writer proposes that the board drawings be published
he asks that parts be sold at what the component costs
the obstacle is commercial and not technical
text: Mending ought to cost less than replacing, and it hardly ever does. The fault lies not with the labour but with the way the things are drawn up. A battery stuck to the frame with adhesive, screws cut to a head nobody else uses, a ribbon soldered where a plug would do: each choice adds half an hour to the job and turns a cell swap into a full strip-down. The reason offered is water resistance; yet a compressed seal and ordinary screws hold water out just as well, at a cost close to nothing. Three measures would be enough: settle on common screws, publish the board drawings, and sell spare parts at what the parts themselves cost. None of them demands a technical leap; all of them run into a trade that lives on replacement. While a sealed device costs less to build than one that opens, the bench will go on unscrewing sealed cases.
